levels.name: Tumbling Rows
levels.tagline: Groups that are all the same size.
levels.cheer: The tumbling team lines up in 3 rows. There are 4 girls in every row. 🤸
levels.question: How many girls in all?
hints: Add one row at a time: 4 + 4 + 4.

levels.name: Twirl Count
levels.tagline: Jump by 5s instead of counting one by one.
levels.cheer: Every dancer spins 5 times in the routine. 6 dancers take the floor. 💃
levels.question: How many spins in all?
hints: Jump by 5 one time for each dancer.

levels.name: Share the Ribbons
levels.tagline: Sharing so everybody gets the same.
levels.cheer: There are 12 spirit ribbons. 2 friends want to share them so both get the same. 🎀
levels.question: How many ribbons does each friend get?
hints: Sharing the same means both piles match.
Hand out one, then one. Then do it again.
6 and 6 makes 12. So each friend gets 6!

levels.question: Will everybody get a partner?
choices: No, one girl is left over
levels.correctChoice: No, one girl is left over
hints: Count them off in twos and see what happens.
9 is an odd number. Odd numbers always leave one out!

teach.heading: Groups that match
teach.body:
A group is a little pile. When every pile is the same size, you can add the same number again and again to find the total.

If 3 dancers each hold 4 pom-poms, that is 4 and 4 and 4.

teach.heading: They have to be equal
teach.body:
This only works if every group is the same size.

If one girl has 4 ribbons, one has 7, and one has 2, the piles do not match. You just have to add them the long way.

teach.heading: Say it out loud
teach.body:
Say "3 groups of 4." Saying it helps you picture it.

Then count the groups one at a time. Do not rush.

practice.prompt: One dancer has 3 bows. One has 6 bows. One has 1 bow.
practice.question: Are these equal groups?
choices: No, the piles are different sizes
practice.correct: No, the piles are different sizes
practice.explain: 3, 6 and 1 do not match. Equal groups all have to be the same size.

practice.question: How many groups of 4 is that?
practice.explain: Count the 4s. There are three of them. 3 groups of 4.

practice.question: What does she mean?
practice.explain: 2 groups of 5 means a 5 and another 5. That is 10.

reinforce.prompt: A pile has 2. Another has 2. Another has 9.
reinforce.question: Are these equal groups?
reinforce.explain: 9 does not match the 2s, so the groups are not equal.

reinforce.question: How many groups of 2?
reinforce.explain: Count the 2s. There are four. 4 groups of 2 makes 8.

lessons.title: Skip counting
lessons.subtitle: A faster way to count groups.

teach.heading: Jump. Do not crawl.
teach.body:
You do not have to count every single thing one at a time.

You can jump. To count groups of 5, jump by 5.

teach.heading: One jump is one group
teach.body:
Every jump you take is one more group.

Jump by 5 four times and you have counted 4 groups of 5.

teach.heading: Start with the easy jumps
teach.body:
Twos, fives and tens are the easiest to jump.

Learn those three and you can count almost anything fast.

practice.prompt: Start at 0 and jump by 5, four times.
practice.question: Where do you land?
What comes next?
practice.explain: You are jumping by 2. After 8 comes 10.

practice.question: What comes next?
practice.explain: You are jumping by 10. After 30 comes 40.

reinforce.prompt: Jump by 2 five times, starting at 0.
reinforce.question: Where do you land?
What comes next?
reinforce.explain: You are jumping by 5. After 15 comes 20.

reinforce.prompt: Jump by 10 three times, starting at 0.
reinforce.question: Where do you land?

lessons.title: Rows and columns
lessons.subtitle: Lining things up makes it easy.

teach.heading: Every row is a group
teach.body:
When things line up in neat rows, each row is a group.

Count one row. Then add that number again for every other row.

teach.heading: It works both ways
teach.body:
You can count across the rows, or down the columns.

You get the same answer either way. Try it and see.

teach.heading: That is a handy trick
teach.body:
If one way feels hard, turn it around.

2 rows of 5 might be easier than 5 rows of 2. Both give you 10.

practice.prompt: The squad lines up in 3 rows. Each row has 5 girls.
practice.question: How many girls?

practice.prompt: Someone says 2 rows of 5 and 5 rows of 2 give different totals.
practice.question: Are they right?
practice.explain: Turning it around does not change the total. Both make 10.

practice.prompt: You find 5 rows of 2 hard, but you are good at fives.
practice.question: What is the easier way?

reinforce.prompt: Does 4 rows of 3 give the same total as 3 rows of 4?
reinforce.question: Same or different?
reinforce.explain: Rows or columns, you land on 12 either way.

teach.heading: Sharing fairly
teach.body:
Sharing fairly means everybody ends up with the same amount.

If 12 ribbons are shared by 2 girls, hand them out one at a time until they are gone. Both piles will match.

teach.heading: Nobody gets extra
teach.body:
It is only a fair share if the piles are equal.

One girl cannot take 8 while the other gets 4. That is not sharing.

teach.heading: Check by putting it back
teach.body:
Finished sharing? Add the piles back up.

If you get the number you started with, you did it right.

practice.prompt: 10 medals are shared by 2 gymnasts. Both get the same.
practice.question: How many each?

practice.prompt: 8 girls need to make lines of 2.
practice.question: How many lines?

practice.prompt: 10 candies. One girl takes 7. The other gets 3.
practice.question: Is that a fair share?
choices: No, the piles are not equal
practice.correct: No, the piles are not equal
practice.explain: 7 and 3 do not match. A fair share would be 5 and 5.

reinforce.prompt: 9 stickers. One girl takes 6, the other takes 3.
reinforce.question: Fair share?
reinforce.explain: 6 and 3 do not match, so it is not a fair share.

teach.heading: Pair them up
teach.body:
Take any number of girls and pair them up two by two.

If everybody gets a partner, that number is even. If one is left standing, it is odd.
teach.example: 8 → 4 pairs, nobody left  ·  9 → 4 pairs and 1 left

teach.heading: Even numbers
teach.body:
Even numbers always pair up perfectly.

2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 are even. So is every number you land on when you jump by 2.

teach.heading: Look at the last digit
teach.body:
You do not have to pair up a big number to know.

Just look at the very last digit. If it ends in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8, the number is even.
teach.example: 14 ends in 4 → even  ·  17 ends in 7 → odd

practice.prompt: 7 cheerleaders pair up two by two.
practice.question: Does everybody get a partner?
practice.explain: 7 is odd. Odd numbers always leave one out.

practice.question: Odd or even?
practice.explain: 12 ends in 2, so it is even.

practice.question: How many pairs?
practice.explain: 6 pairs up into 3 twos, with nobody left over.

practice.question: Odd or even?
practice.explain: 15 ends in 5, so it is odd.

reinforce.question: Anyone left over?
reinforce.explain: 10 is even, so it pairs up perfectly.

reinforce.question: Odd or even?
reinforce.explain: 9 ends in 9, so it is odd.

reinforce.question: Odd or even?
reinforce.explain: 20 ends in 0, so it is even.
